scenes.heading: Experimental probability
scenes.sub: When you can’t work it out, test it!
scenes.say: What's the chance a bottle cap lands top up? There's no neat list of equally likely outcomes. So we experiment, count what happens, and use the results to estimate the probability.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A café tests a new muffin on lots of customers and counts who buys it again
scenes.science: Experimental probability: run many trials and count the successes
scenes.breaks: Customers' tastes can change. In an experiment we assume the chance stays the same each trial.
scenes.say: A café tests a new muffin. After ten customers, it has a rough idea. After five hundred, it's fairly confident. Experimental probability works the same way. You learn the chance by watching what happens, and more trials mean more confidence.

scenes.heading: Experimental probability
scenes.say: Experimental probability is the number of times the event happened, divided by the number of trials.

scenes.heading: Two coins: four outcomes
scenes.say: Before we compare, draw a tree. The first coin is heads or tails. Each branch splits again for the second coin. That gives four outcomes, and one of each happens two ways: H T and T H.
scenes.caption: Four equally likely outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT. One of each happens two ways, so its probability is 1/2.

scenes.heading: Two coins
scenes.question: Two coins tossed 100 times: two heads 22, one of each 53, two tails 25. Compare with theory.
scenes.say: Two coins are tossed a hundred times. List the outcomes: head head, head tail, tail head, tail tail. One of each happens two ways, so its probability is one half. We'd expect twenty-five, fifty and twenty-five. We got twenty-two, fifty-three and twenty-five. That's close.
scenes.caption: Two coins are tossed 100 times. List the outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT. One of each happens two ways, so its probability is 1/2. We'd expect 25, 50 and 25. We got 22, 53 and 25. That's close.

scenes.heading: Pool the data
scenes.question: Four groups flip a bottle cap 25 times each. Top up: 9, 12, 8, 11. Best estimate?
scenes.say: Four groups each flip a bottle cap twenty-five times. Their results vary a lot. So pool the data: forty top up out of a hundred flips. The best estimate is zero point four.
scenes.caption: Four groups each flip a bottle cap 25 times. Their results vary a lot. So pool the data: 40 top up out of 100 flips. The best estimate is 0.4.

scenes.heading: Is the spinner fair?
notes: Fair: about 50 of each in 200 spins
scenes.say: A four-section spinner was spun two hundred times. Fair would be about fifty each. The bars for one, two and four are close to fifty, but three shot up to seventy-two. That suggests the spinner is biased towards three.
scenes.caption: Fair would give about 50 of each. 3 came up 72 times, so P(3) ≈ 0.36: the spinner may be biased.

scenes.heading: Running a simulation
steps: Pick a device with the same chance
scenes.say: To run a simulation, find the real probability. Pick a device with the same chance, like a coin for one half or a die for one sixth. Decide what one trial is. Then repeat it many times and count the results.

points: Pool data for a better estimate
Judge fairness only after many trials
scenes.say: Recap. Experimental probability is successes divided by trials. List every outcome in two-step experiments. Pool data for a better estimate. And only judge fairness after many trials. Now try the practice questions!
